pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-chee-mahn' — the 'ch' is crisp, and the final 'n' is a soft closed nasal.

pronunciation.note: Hachiman is Tier 2: the name is plain Hepburn. His importance is institutional and martial, not orthographic.

domains.title: God of War, Archery, and Divine Protection
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Nation and the Samurai
domains.lead: Hachiman is the kami of war, archery, and protection, worshipped by samurai, peasants, and emperors alike. His symbol — eight banners (hachi-man) — recalls the standards under which the divine child grew to become a warrior patron. He is one of the most widely enshrined kami in Japan, and his cult blurred the boundary between Shinto and Buddhism for over a millennium.

cards.name: War God
cards.desc: Patron of warriors, archers, and those who fight in defense of order.

cards.name: Eight Banners
cards.desc: His name refers to the eight ritual banners that accompanied his divine birth.

cards.name: Divine Protector
cards.desc: Guardian of the nation, invoked by the imperial house and local communities.

cards.name: Shinbutsu Synthesis
cards.desc: Worshipped both as a kami and as the Buddhist bodhisattva Hachiman Daibosatsu.

mythology.lead: Hachiman's mythology is entangled with imperial history. He is most commonly identified as the deified Emperor Ōjin, making him a kami who was once a man — and a model of martial devotion.

myths.title: The Deified Emperor Ōjin
myths.text: Emperor Ōjin, the 15th emperor, was posthumously worshipped as Hachiman after his death in the 4th century. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki describe his mother, Empress Jingū, conquering Korea while pregnant with him; he was born on campaign and grew into a ruler who promoted Korean culture and technology. His deification made him a divine ancestor of war and statecraft.

myths.title: Guardian of the North
myths.text: The great shrine at Usa in Kyūshū became Hachiman's principal cult center. In the 8th century the shrine's oracle supported the imperial move of the capital and the suppression of the Emi rebellion. Hachiman was thus drawn into the political center: a regional war god became protector of the realm.

myths.title: Hachiman Daibosatsu
myths.text: In medieval Japan, Hachiman was identified with the Buddhist bodhisattva Hachiman Daibosatsu. Major temples such as Tōdai-ji housed shrines to him, and samurai clans claimed his protection before battle. The fusion of kami and bodhisattva was only dismantled by the Meiji separation of Shinto and Buddhism.

lore.syncretism: Hachiman is the archetype of shinbutsu shūgō, the medieval blending of kami and Buddhist cult. As Emperor Ōjin he is human, ancestral, and imperial; as Hachiman Daibosatsu he is universal, compassionate, and warlike. This double identity made him indispensable to the samurai state and to local communities seeking protection.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hachiman shrines are found throughout Japan, from the great Usa Jingū and Iwashimizu Hachimangū to neighborhood shrines that bear his name. He is the tutelary kami of the Minamoto clan and of countless warrior houses. Sumo, archery, and the martial arts invoke him, and his image appears in festival floats, emblems, and military insignia.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hachiman asks what it means to fight with divine sanction. He is not a god of aggression but of protection — the warrior who defends the realm. His eight banners remind us that war, when it comes, should be ordered, ritualized, and directed toward preservation rather than conquest.

sources.name: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (Emperor Ōjin narratives)
Grapard, The Protocol of the Gods

lore.archaeology: Usa Jingū in Ōita is Hachiman's head shrine, with a long history documented in shrine records and archaeology. Iwashimizu Hachimangū near Kyōto was built as a guardian shrine for the capital. Tōdai-ji's Hachiman shrine preserves the Buddhist-Shinto synthesis of the Nara period.
